title: Designs that other teams must live with
summary: A boundary is a contract and an operating responsibility, not just a box.

steps.title: A shared API changes under three teams
steps.text: Your team renames a response field. The website updates, but a billing job and an old mobile client fail overnight. The data shape was an informal contract even though nobody wrote it down. A design crosses team boundaries whenever another team must depend on its behavior, availability or change schedule.

steps.title: Put authority with an owner
steps.text: Choose boundaries around coherent data and invariants, access patterns and the teams able to operate them. Name the authoritative writer and the on-call owner for each dataset and API. Shared ownership without a decision rule can mean nobody owns recovery. Too many tiny services spread a single invariant across network calls; a huge shared service can make every change a negotiation. Use an internal module when it preserves cohesion without requiring independent deployment. A service boundary earns its cost when it creates useful autonomy, security or scaling isolation. Include dashboards, runbooks and dependency failure behavior in the contract.

steps.title: Worked example: the on-call bill
steps.text: Assume four services each produce two actionable pages a week, and each page consumes 45 minutes including follow-up. That is eight pages and six hours/week, or about 312 hours/year. If only three engineers can operate the stack, those pages and recovery work constrain delivery. Combining services will not automatically remove pages; eliminating duplicated failure paths or clarifying ownership might. For an API deprecation with 200 callers, suppose 180 migrate in month one. The last 20 may include the least observable batch jobs. Count actual endpoint use and caller identity rather than declaring 90% migration complete enough. This is an operating model, not a simulated page count.

rows.label: Remaining callers
rows.how: 200 - 180; risk depends on which callers remain

steps.q: Three teams write the same table and each thinks another owns recovery. What should the design settle?
choices: Authoritative write rules, recovery owner and change process
steps.why: Ownership is behavior and operational responsibility, not a label alone.

steps.q: Where would you split this service? Follow-up: another team needs to change independently.
checklist: Start with invariant and authoritative data ownership
Balance independent deployment against coordination cost
steps.model: I would first map the writes that must commit together and who can operate them. A separate team can own a coherent capability through an API without directly mutating another team's tables. If that boundary splits an invariant, we need a redesigned workflow or must keep the transaction together. I would document data authority, versioning, failure behavior and on-call before treating independent deployment as a benefit. A module boundary may be enough until the operating case is clear.

steps.title: Write a document people can disagree with
steps.text: Start with the problem, user promises, explicit non-goals and measured constraints. Show one request path, data ownership and the key invariant. Record alternatives and why they lost, then failures, costs, security boundaries, rollout and open questions. Ask reviewers to challenge a specific decision. API contracts need field semantics, error states, idempotency, rate limits and compatibility rules; data contracts need schema, meaning, freshness and deletion behavior. Prefer additive changes, tolerant readers where safe and explicit versions for incompatible meaning. Publish deprecation dates, contact owners, instrument use, offer a migration path and test old clients. Stop only with evidence that consumers have moved or an agreed exception policy. An empty dashboard is not proof if an annual job has not run.

steps.q: Ninety percent of API callers migrated. Can the endpoint be removed?
choices: Only after remaining callers are identified and migrated or covered by agreed policy
steps.why: A small number of important or infrequent consumers can still make removal unsafe.

steps.q: How will you deprecate an API used by teams you do not know? Follow-up: one annual caller never appears in the last month's logs.
checklist: Instrument caller identity and consult the owner registry
Provide compatibility, deadlines and migration support
Account for infrequent jobs and an exception process
steps.model: I would inventory consumers from credentials, code references, owners and telemetry, then publish the replacement and a support window. Usage logs are evidence, but a month misses annual jobs. I would ask identified owners to test the replacement and check schedules, run a controlled warning phase and keep an explicit exception owner. Removal needs a decision about the remaining risk. I would record that decision so a future on-call engineer does not have to reconstruct it during an outage.

steps.q: Two actions must preserve one local transaction invariant and are owned by one team. What is a reasonable starting boundary?
choices: One cohesive module or service, unless another requirement justifies splitting
Separate services for each table by default
A shared writable database with no authority
steps.why: A network boundary adds failure and coordination. It should serve an actual ownership or scaling need.

takeaway: Name the invariant, the owner and the compatibility promise before drawing a team boundary.
